rules.statement: TEMPO: fluctuations lasting 30 minutes to less than 60 minutes.
rules.section: TAF guide, significant changes and variations

rules.statement: INTER: fluctuations lasting less than 30 minutes.
rules.section: TAF guide, significant changes and variations

rules.statement: When PROB is used with thunderstorms without INTER or TEMPO, the likely period of occurrence is deemed to be one hour or more; the guide states this for thunderstorms only.
TAF3 in the remarks marks a TAF3: issued every 3 hours, reviewed in depth hourly with priority amendments, 24/7 at the major airports including Adelaide; VALID TL marks the end of a limited service.

FM begins a self-contained forecast that applies until the end of the TAF or the next FM/BECMG; BECMG is a change at an unspecified time within its period; TEMPO/INTER are variations from the prevailing conditions.
rules.section: TAF guide, significant changes and variations (FM, BECMG, INTER, TEMPO)

rules.statement: CAVOK: visibility 10 km or more, no cloud below 5 000 ft or the highest 25 NM MSA (whichever is higher) and no CB/TCU, no significant weather.
rules.section: TAF guide and METAR/SPECI guide, CAVOK

rules.statement: Ceiling: the height of the base of the lowest layer of cloud below 20 000 ft covering more than half the sky (BKN or OVC).
rules.section: CASR Dictionary definition, applied in Part 121 MOS 2020 s 4.06; BoM METAR/SPECI guide, cloud

rules.statement: For larger aeroplanes forecast cloud amounts below the relevant ceiling are cumulative: FEW+FEW=SCT, FEW+SCT=BKN, SCT+SCT=BKN or OVC.
AIRMET covers phenomena below 10 000 ft not already in the GAF, including isolated or occasional thunderstorms and moderate turbulence, icing and mountain waves.
A SIGMET level group is in feet AMSL or flight levels as written (FLnnn, nnnnFT, SFC/, TOP, ABV, BLW).
METAR and TAF wind directions are degrees true; runway designators are magnetic. Variation: YSSY 13°E, YPPH 2°W (ERSA FAC, 03 SEP 2026).
rules.section: METAR/SPECI guide, wind; AIP ERSA FAC YSSY and YPPH

rules.statement: SIGMETs are issued for OBSC/EMBD/FRQ/SQL TS (with or without GR), TC, SEV TURB, SEV ICE (incl. FZRA), SEV MTW, HVY DS/SS, VA and radioactive cloud; turbulence and icing only when severe.
A SIGMET is valid for no more than 4 hours; volcanic ash and tropical cyclone SIGMETs for no more than 6 hours; it is cancelled when the phenomenon is no longer occurring or expected.
The destination/alternate forecast must be valid from at least 30 minutes before to 60 minutes after the planned ETA.
If the required destination forecast is not available, a destination alternate must be nominated.

Relevant weather: cloud more than SCT below the alternate minima; visibility below them, or at/above them with a ≥30% probability of fog, mist, dust or another phenomenon reducing it below them; wind components beyond the aircraft maximum; a thunderstorm or associated severe turbulence, or a ≥30% probability of one.

Part 91: on a TAF3 with the ETA in its first 3 hours and inside the service, probabilities may be ignored (s 8.02 (2)) and the alternate window is the forecast period itself, without the 30 min buffers (s 8.04 (2)). Part 121: the PROB period must be within the first 3 hours and no part of the time of use after the service end (s 4.06 (7)); AC 121-11 3.4.11.1 frames it as the time of use wholly within the first 3 hours.
An alternate is required when the ETA falls from 30 minutes before the forecast start to 30 minutes after the forecast end of relevant weather.
The weather alternate rule does not apply to a VFR flight by day within 50 NM of the departure aerodrome.
No alternate is needed if fuel is carried to hold until 30 minutes after the forecast end of the relevant weather.
For relevant weather forecast INTER, 30 minutes of holding fuel; TEMPO, 60 minutes; with several indicators, the most limiting.
A BECMG deterioration applies from the start of the BECMG period; an improvement in all elements applies from its end.
An IFR flight to a destination without an IAP the pilot can conduct, or a night VFR flight, needs a destination alternate unless the exceptions in s 8.05 apply.

Night: pilot-activated lighting needs a responsible person to switch it on manually or an alternate, or fuel to hold until first light plus 10 minutes; a single-VHF aircraft may nominate a PAL alternate only with a responsible person arranged, HF and 30 minutes holding fuel.
An alternate must not itself be an aerodrome for which the aircraft would require an alternate; holding fuel that removes that requirement (e.g. 60 minutes for a TEMPO) makes it usable.
Alternate minima: the published IAP alternate minima; without them, the table in s 8.08 (1).

Fuel to be carried: taxi, trip, destination alternate, holding if required, contingency, final reserve and additional if applicable; Part 91 makes alternate and holding conditional and contingency N/A for piston or turboprop aeroplanes of 5 700 kg MTOW or less.
Discretionary fuel is an extra amount carried at the discretion of the PIC; anticipated holding is holding fuel, a required component.
rules.section: AC 91-15 para 1.2; Part 121 MOS 2020 s 1.04, holding fuel

rules.statement: Additional fuel covers engine failure or depressurisation at the critical point: proceed to an alternate, hold 15 minutes at 1 500 ft, approach and land.

Final reserve fuel: 30 minutes (turbine) or 45 minutes (piston) at holding speed at 1 500 ft above the aerodrome in ISA, at the estimated arrival weight; usable fuel remaining on completion of the final landing.
rules.section: Part 121 MOS 2020 s 1.04, final reserve fuel; Part 91 MOS 2020 s 19.02

rules.statement: MINIMUM FUEL when committed to a landing with less than final reserve projected; MAYDAY FUEL when the usable fuel on landing will be less than final reserve.
Contingency fuel: 5% of trip fuel (turbine) or 10% (piston), but not less than 5 minutes at holding speed at 1 500 ft above the destination in ISA.

Destination alternate fuel: missed approach, climb, cruise, descent, approach and landing at the alternate; without an alternate, 15 minutes at holding speed at 1 500 ft; at an isolated aerodrome, 2 hours at normal cruise consumption (turbine) including final reserve.
If a flight is re-planned in flight, the fuel required from the point of re-planning must again meet the fuel requirements.
Radiation fog needs clear skies, moist air near the surface and light winds (about 5 kt or less); it forms overnight and clears with heating or wind.
Advection fog forms when moist air moves over a cooler surface and can persist with winds of 6–18 kt.
A thunderstorm needs instability, moisture and a lifting trigger. (CAPE is not defined in the guide; cards state its definition without citing it.)
A downburst gives a strong headwind, then the downdraft, then a strong tailwind; it is distinct from the broader gust front.

Clear ice forms from large supercooled droplets at about 0 to −10 °C, typically in cumuliform cloud; rime from small droplets at about −10 to −20 °C in stratiform cloud; freezing rain gives the most severe icing; hoar frost can form in clear air; severe icing calls for an immediate change of heading and/or altitude.
DALR about 3 °C per 1 000 ft, SALR about 1.5 °C per 1 000 ft; absolutely stable when ELR < SALR, conditionally unstable between SALR and DALR, absolutely unstable above DALR.
rules.section: Atmospheric stability and the aerological diagram guide

rules.statement: Geostrophic wind: pressure gradient force balanced by Coriolis force along straight isobars; closer isobars mean a stronger wind; Buys Ballot: in the southern hemisphere with your back to the wind, low pressure is on the right; friction turns the surface wind towards the low (a veer in the southern hemisphere).
rules.section: Aviation glossary, geostrophic wind and Buys Ballot's law; Manual of Aviation Meteorology, wind

rules.statement: QNH is station pressure reduced to mean sea level so the altimeter reads aerodrome elevation on the ground; reported in whole hectopascals rounded down; reduction over terrain uses an assumed air column.
rules.section: Area QNH guide; METAR/SPECI guide, QNH

rules.statement: IFR: a pressure altitude system must read site elevation within 60 ft; 60 to 75 ft allows flight to the first landing for a recheck; more than 75 ft is inoperative.
Cold fronts across southern Australia bring a wind change from north-westerly to south-westerly with a pressure rise; pre-frontal troughs and sea breezes are the common triggers for convection.
rules.section: Flying in south-western and south-eastern Australia guides
